book.title: Cultures of War: Pearl Harbor/Hiroshima/9-11/Iraq

evidence: trade publisher signal: W. W. Norton / W. W. Norton & Company

argument.statement: The cultures of war across these events reveal recurring pathologies—intelligence and imagination failures, strategic “imbecilities,” targeting noncombatants, and an alluring logic of mass destruction.

book.rationale: The book primarily examines the dynamics and consequences of war, positioning it clearly within the War & Military subject, with significant connections to American History due to its focus on U.S. events.
book.summary: Finalist for the 2010 National Book Award in Nonfiction: The Pulitzer Prize-winning historian returns with a groundbreaking comparative study of the dynamics and pathologies of war in modern times. Over recent decades, John W. Dower, one of America’s preeminent historians, has addressed the roots and consequences of war from multiple perspectives. In War Without Mercy (1986), winner of the National Book Critics Circle Award, he described and analyzed the brutality that attended World War II in the Pacific, as seen from both the Japanese and the American sides. Embracing Defeat (1999), winner of numerous honors including the Pulitzer Prize and the National Book Award, dealt with Japan’s struggle to start over in a shattered land in the immediate aftermath of the Pacific War, when the defeated country was occupied by the U.S.-led Allied powers. Turning to an even larger canvas, Dower now examines the cultures of war revealed by four powerful events—Pearl Harbor, Hiroshima, 9-11, and the invasion of Iraq in the name of a war on terror. The list of issues examined and themes explored is wide-ranging: failures of intelligence and imagination, wars of choice and “strategic imbecilities,” faith-based secular thinking as well as more overtly holy wars, the targeting of noncombatants, and the almost irresistible logic—and allure—of mass destruction.
